title: How Origami Solves One of Space Travel's Biggest Problems
description: AI-narrated commentary on how origami math -- the Miura fold -- shaped real spacecraft engineering, from satellite solar panels to the James Webb Space Telescope's mirror. Original commentary, not affiliated with or based on any single source video.

hook_candidates.text: How do you fit a solar array the size of a tennis court into a rocket smaller than a delivery van?
The same fold you learned in grade-school origami is now protecting billion-dollar satellites in orbit.
Origami isn't a kids' craft -- it's literally how engineers solve one of space travel's hardest problems.

beats.text: How do you fit a solar array the size of a tennis court into a rocket smaller than a delivery van?
Engineers stole the answer from an ancient paper craft: origami.
The Miura fold, invented by an astrophysicist, collapses flat into a tiny stack that springs open instantly.
NASA used that exact math to design solar panels that pack flat for launch, then unfurl to power entire satellites.

beats.text: The James Webb Space Telescope's massive mirror folds the same way just to survive the trip.
Even future Mars habitats are being designed to fold flat and pop open like a tent, cutting launch costs dramatically.
So next time you fold paper, you're doing rocket science. What other 'kid stuff' secretly built our world? Tell me below.
